rules.when: The project is written in JavaScript.

use.layout: `src/` for source, `test/` mirroring it, `bin/` for executables, one entry file at the package root.
use.practices: Small single-purpose modules, no build step without a measured need, a test beside the module it covers, never commit `node_modules`.

rules.why: Node resolves from the package root, so a shallow documented tree beats a deep one.

rules.when: The project is written in TypeScript.

use.layout: `src/` for source, `test/` mirroring it, shared types in `src/types/` only when more than one module uses them.
use.practices: `strict` on, no `any` at a trust boundary, types beside their implementation, one compile target.

rules.why: Strict types with colocated declarations stop the type surface drifting from the code.

rules.when: The project is written in Python.

use.layout: `<package>/` for the importable package, `tests/` for tests, one `pyproject.toml` at the root for packaging and tool config.
use.practices: An isolated virtualenv, type hints on public functions, `ruff` for lint and format, no logic in `__init__.py`.

rules.why: One pyproject plus a real package directory is the layout every tool already expects.

rules.when: The project is written in Go.

use.layout: `cmd/<binary>/` for entry points, `internal/` for private packages, `pkg/` only for genuinely reusable code.
use.practices: Return errors rather than panicking, accept interfaces and return structs, table-driven `_test.go` beside the package.

rules.why: `internal/` makes the public surface a deliberate choice rather than an accident.

default.why: No layout is preferred. Follow the best practice for the language in use, then add a rule above when a layout should hold across projects.
